h1:
Samut Prakan on a Budget
BTS, Ferry & Cheap Eats
intro: Samut Prakan is one of the best-value day trips near Bangkok, mostly because the Green Line BTS runs all the way down to Pak Nam. Step off the train and you can walk on or hop a ferry that costs only a few baht, and the food at the old markets still goes for the old prices — 30 THB noodles really are out there. We put together a 2-day plan that keeps spending as low as possible, with no car needed, using public transport the whole way.

blocks.html: A lot of people assume you need to drive to visit Samut Prakan, but the Green Line BTS actually runs to its southern terminus at Kheha station, passing right through the middle of Pak Nam on the way. That means you can do the whole trip without ever touching a steering wheel. Your main costs come down to the BTS fare, the ferry, and food — and together that easily stays in the low hundreds of baht per day if you pick spots that are free or cheap to enter.

blocks.text: How to get around for the least money

blocks.html: The backbone of a budget trip is the Green Line BTS. The northern end is Khu Khot and the southern end is Kheha, so you can ride straight down from central Bangkok to the Samut Prakan side. The stations you'll use most are Pu Chao (the Erawan elephant is near here), Chang Erawan, Pak Nam (for the old town and ferry pier), and Kheha at the very end.

items: Green Line BTS — gets you to Pak Nam, the Erawan Museum, and the observation tower. Fares are by distance, and the Samut Prakan end of the line has a fairly low fare cap.
Pak Nam–Phra Samut Chedi ferry — 8 THB per trip (4 THB for students and uniformed officials), runs daily with the last boat around 9.30 pm. It's just a few minutes across the Chao Phraya River.
Motorbike taxi from Pak Nam station — around 15 THB to Pak Nam market if you don't feel like walking.
Songthaew / local bus — useful for getting from the stations to places the BTS doesn't reach, like the Bang Phli side, for a few tens of baht.

blocks.title: Money-saving trick
blocks.html: If you're heading out from Bangkok, top up a Rabbit card once and you're set — no queuing for tokens at every station. And take the train home outside rush hour in the evening; it's far more comfortable.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Pak Nam, the ferry, and Phra Samut Chedi

blocks.html: Day one focuses on the Pak Nam old town, a zone where almost everything is free or cheap to enter. The highlight is taking the ferry across the Chao Phraya to pay respects at Phra Samut Chedi — the boat costs only single-digit baht, but you get the full riverside atmosphere.

items.activity: Take the BTS to Pak Nam station
items.note: Head out a bit early to beat the midday heat while walking the market

items.activity: Walk or grab a motorbike taxi to Pak Nam market for breakfast
items.note: Fresh market with souvenirs and dried goods; about 15 THB by motorbike taxi from the station

items.activity: Head to the pier and take the ferry to Phra Samut Chedi
items.note: 8 THB per trip, just a few minutes across

items.activity: Visit Phra Samut Chedi and walk the riverside
items.note: Free entry; the white chedi stands out right on the Chao Phraya

items.activity: Take the ferry back to the Pak Nam side for lunch
items.note: The market side has plenty of rice and noodle shops

items.activity: Stop by the Samut Prakan observation tower / learning park on the Pak Nam side
items.note: Close to the station; check opening hours before you go

items.activity: Ride the BTS back, or carry on to Day 2
items.note: Avoid the BTS rush hour of 5–7 pm

blocks.text: Day 2 — Erawan, Bang Krachao, and the old market

blocks.html: On day two you can choose to go cultural around the Erawan Museum, or go for nature and cycle around Bang Krachao. The plan below is a budget mix of both zones. If money is really tight, the Erawan elephant looks great from the outside — entry to the inside runs about 250 THB for a Thai adult, so decide on the spot.

items.activity: BTS to Chang Erawan station, visit the Erawan Museum
items.note: Entry around 250 THB for Thai adults, 125 THB for children, open 9 am–6 pm · photos outside are free

items.activity: Take the BTS plus a connecting ride to the Phra Pradaeng side, into Bang Krachao
Rent a bike and ride around Bang Krachao
items.note: Around 30 THB/hr or 100 THB for the whole day

items.activity: Stop at Bang Nam Phueng floating market for lunch
items.note: Open weekends only, 8 am–2:30 pm; cheap food all along the canal

items.activity: Leave Bang Krachao, stop at Bang Phli old market if there's time
items.note: A market over 100 years old; noodles start at 30 THB
From the Bang Phli side you can connect to BTS On Nut or a station on the Samut Prakan side

blocks.text: Cheap eats that locals actually eat

blocks.html: Samut Prakan's draw is old-market food that hasn't climbed to city prices. We picked dishes and shops that locals genuinely eat at, where a plate still costs anywhere from a few tens of baht to the low hundreds.

items.name: Old-style pork noodles, Bang Phli old market
items.blurb: Old-recipe noodles in the historic market by Samrong canal. A regular bowl starts dirt cheap; add a bit extra to fill it out. The best-value lunch of the trip.
items.meta: Bang Phli old market · open weekends

items.name: Pak Mo noodles, Je Aor, Bang Phli
items.blurb: A shop in the Bang Phli old floating market serving steamed pak mo noodles and wide rice noodles in clear pork broth. Locals stop here all the time, and you'll spend under 100 THB a head.

items.name: Rice & curry / dried goods, Pak Nam market
items.blurb: The fresh market in the middle of Pak Nam, with cart-style curry-over-rice stalls plus dried goods and souvenirs. Walk from Pak Nam station or take a 15 THB motorbike taxi.
items.meta: Pak Nam market · near BTS Pak Nam

items.name: Khanom jeen & snacks, Bang Nam Phueng floating market
items.blurb: A canalside market in Bang Krachao with old-style khanom jeen, tom yum noodles, and Thai sweets to graze on as you stroll. Market prices — perfect after a bike ride.
items.meta: Bang Nam Phueng floating market · weekends

items.name: Seafood & made-to-order, Pak Nam side
items.blurb: Pak Nam sits at the river mouth, so made-to-order and seafood spots at local prices are scattered along the waterfront. Pick a busy one and it'll be good value and fresh.

items.name: Sweets & snacks, Bang Phli old market
items.blurb: The old market has several traditional Thai sweets, snacks, and nibbles. Graze your way through a bit at a time, paying just a few baht each.

blocks.title: About market opening days
blocks.html: Bang Nam Phueng floating market and the lively buzz of Bang Phli old market are at their best on weekends. Come on a weekday and a lot of stalls are closed, so we'd plan this trip for a Saturday or Sunday.
These figures are for one person and don't include the BTS fare to and from your own home. It's just a frame so you can see how low you can keep the spending.

items: Ferry round trip — about 16 THB (8 THB each way)
Motorbike taxi / local rides in town — about 30–60 THB/day
Bike rental in Bang Krachao — 100 THB for the day or 30 THB/hr
Three meals — about 150–250 THB if you eat at the markets
Erawan Museum entry (if you go inside) — around 250 THB for a Thai adult · nothing if you only look from outside

blocks.html: Bottom line: skip the museum entry fee and you can genuinely do a day here on a low-hundreds-of-baht budget — and if you do want to go inside the Erawan elephant, it's just that one ticket on top.

faq.q: Can you visit Samut Prakan without a car?
faq.a: Easily. The Green Line BTS runs down to Pak Nam in the middle of town and ends at Kheha station. The main sights — the Erawan Museum, the observation tower, and the Pak Nam old town — are all near stations. For spots the BTS doesn't reach, a motorbike taxi or songthaew costs only a few tens of baht.

faq.q: How much is the Pak Nam–Phra Samut Chedi ferry?
faq.a: Right now it's 8 THB per trip for the general public, or 4 THB for students and uniformed officials. It runs daily with the last boat around 9.30 pm, and crossing the Chao Phraya takes just a few minutes.

faq.q: Where's the cheap, good food in Samut Prakan?
faq.a: The old markets are the answer. Bang Phli old market has old-style pork noodles from 30 THB a bowl, Pak Nam market has curry-over-rice stalls, and Bang Nam Phueng floating market in Bang Krachao has khanom jeen and snacks for tens of baht. They're busiest on weekends.

faq.q: Should I come on a weekday or weekend?
faq.a: If you want the markets lively, come Saturday or Sunday — Bang Nam Phueng floating market only opens on weekends (8 am–2:30 pm) and Bang Phli old market has far more stalls open then. The Erawan Museum and the ferry run every day.

faq.q: How many days does this trip need?
faq.a: Two days is just right. Day one covers the Pak Nam side and the ferry to Phra Samut Chedi, and day two covers the Erawan Museum, Bang Krachao, and the old market. If you only have one day, pick one zone and you'll still have a great time.
